item.title: An age calculator for high-latitude Quaternary foraminifera using amino acid racemization
item.dc:creator: Darrell S. Kaufman, Scarlett Hunt, Joshua Smith, Jordon E. Bright, Claus‐Dieter Hillenbrand, Johann Philipp Klages, … (+4)
item.description:
Scientific Reports — matched: polar, Arctic, Southern Ocean, marine isotope stage, Quaternary, sediment core, foraminifera
Dating deep-sea cores from polar regions is challenging because sedimentation rates can be variable and oxygen-isotope stratigraphy can be ineffective, making amino acid racemization an important alternative. We calibrated the rate of racemization in Neogloboquadrina pachyderma , the dominant high-latitude planktic foraminifer, using 140 independently dated samples from 21 Arctic, Nordic Seas, North Atlantic, and Southern Ocean sites spanning 2 ka to 1.4 Ma. Racemization rates among these ocean basins differ less than among individual sites. Ages are based on aspartic acid, a more precise chronometer than glutamic acid, which, however, provides an independent check on the analysis. A publicly available age calculator returns formal uncertainty intervals incorporating calibration and measurement errors. Ages carry a realistic uncertainty of roughly ± 32% (66% level), insufficient to assign a sample to a specific Marine Isotope Stage but still useful for many polar marine sediment cores. A single age picks correctly between two candidate ages 90% of the time when they differ by a factor of 2.3 (e.g., 100 versus 230 ka). An independently dated horizon in the same core can reduce the uncertainty to ± 28%. Because comparisons are more precise than absolute ages, amino acid geochronology is best applied as a down-core series.

item.title: Last glacial North Pacific oxygenation due to North Atlantic circulation changes
item.dc:creator: Martin Tetard, Alexandre Pohl, Yusuke Okazaki, Andy Ridgwell, Ekaterina Ovsepyan, Luc Beaufort
item.description:
Nature Geoscience — matched: Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, overturning circulation, proxy, foraminifera, Earth system
Nature Geoscience, Published online: 23 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02122-x Transient weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation during the last glacial period may have led to a contraction of oxygen minimum zones in the North Pacific, according to benthic foraminifera proxy records and Earth system simulations.

item.title: Estimating the impact of ice-sheet surface height and ice-divide variability on ice-core based climate reconstructions
item.dc:creator: Christian Wirths, Kyung-Sook Yun, Axel Timmermann, Hubertus Fischer, Thomas F. Stocker, Johannes C. R. Sutter
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, Antarctica
Ice drilled from deep inside Antarctica reveals how climate changed over hundreds of thousands of years. However, the ice sheet itself rises and sinks over time, which can distort temperatures read from the ice. Using three computer simulations covering the last two million years, we show that drilling sites rose and sank by up to 240 metres and their summits shifted by up to 120 kilometres, and we estimate how this biases climate records, including potential for the oldest ice.

item.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
item.dc:creator: Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio S\'anchez-Ben\'itez, … (+1)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: ensemble, downscaling
arXiv:2611.27641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

item.title: Combining geodetic data and summer MODIS albedo anomalies for annual glacier mass balance estimation
item.dc:creator: Mattia Callegari, Carlo Marin, Claudia Notarnicola, Thomas Schellenberger
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, albedo
We introduce a new satellite-based approach to estimate annual glacier mass balance. Using data from 2000 to 2019, we produced yearly estimates for nearly three thousand glaciers in the Alps, Scandinavia, and Svalbard. Comparison with extensive field measurements shows strong agreement, demonstrating that this method can reliably track annual glacier changes across large regions.

item.title: GDDRP-CMIP6: Global Daily Runoff Projections from Bias-Corrected and Downscaled CMIP6 Forcing
item.dc:creator: Jiachao Chen, Dai Yamazaki, Ming Pan
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: CMIP, ensemble
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) High-resolution, bias-corrected runoff from one globally consistent hydrological framework underpins regional hazard-risk studies and cross-regional comparisons. We developed a global daily runoff at 0.25 degree from 9 CMIP6 models. Compared with the raw runoff, it better reproduces seasonality, mean flow and extremes, and offers a consistent historical baseline while keeping ensemble-mean future trends. It can support flood, drought and water studies worldwide.

item.title: Ice thickness of Comox and Kokanee Glaciers, British Columbia, determined through relative gravity surveys
item.dc:creator: Matthew R. G. Forbes, Lucinda J. Leonard
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, sea level, climate change
There is a global lack of data on glaciers, critical for tracking climate change, with implications for freshwater supply and sea level. We measure the ice thickness across 2 glaciers in western Canada by recording and modelling variations in gravity; gravity is lower where low-density ice is thicker. A 50 m mean ice thickness for Kokanee Glacier is consistent with previous numerical and radar studies. Our 42 m mean ice thickness is the first to be determined for Comox Glacier, Vancouver Island.

item.title: Assessment of Zirconium‐Enriched Late Holocene Sediments in the Karstic Yucatan Peninsula as Potential Distal‐Source Inputs Into Lake Kaná, Southeast Mexico
item.dc:creator: Haydar B Martinez-Dyrzo, Priyadarsi Debajyoti Roy, Benjamin Keenan, Irma Gabriela Vargas-Martínez, Daniel Rosas, Luis A. Ladino
item.description:
Geological Journal — matched: Holocene
Source identification of terrigenous fractions in karstic lacustrine archives has always been challenging. Low relief, limited surface drainage and heterogeneous shallow soils in the Yucatan Peninsula of southeast Mexico further complicate the relation between sediment composition and sediment source. Based on a conservative geochemical screening, the recurrent intervals with Zr/Ti × 1000 ≥ 40 (Zr‐enriched deposits) over the Late Holocene from Lake Kaná were considered as candidates for distal‐source inputs at eastern part of the Yucatan Peninsula. Elemental geochemistry determined by energy‐dispersive X‐ray fluorescence (ED‐XRF) was evaluated using threshold‐based, multivariate statistical, and lithogenic‐baseline approaches and compared with a hydroclimate index. This integrated approach identified Zr‐enrichment at ~1650 cal yr. BP, ~1414–1360 cal yr. BP and ~1190–910 cal yr. BP. Some of them were contemporary with phases of dry hydroclimate and in others, the Pb‐rich and compositionally distinct horizons indicated possible Mesoamerican volcanic sources or mixed atmospheric contributions. These results showed recurrent zirconium enrichment in a region and in an interval when the ancient Maya civilization flourished and demised. This possible association with environment has not been considered earlier. The stratigraphic intervals with Zr‐enriched deposits could be suitable candidates for targeted follow‐up analyses to determine the influence of trans‐Atlantic Saharan dust or other distal‐source contributions to the Maya Lowlands over the geological past in the context of modern era African dust dynamics in this region.

item.title: Natural analogs for geoengineering suggest modest radiative plant gains
item.dc:creator: Brendan Clark, Ben Kravitz, Daniele Visoni, Manuel Lerdau
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: overshoot, numerical method, global warming
arXiv:2611.26845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) to limit global warming overshoot would reduce total solar radiation while increasing the proportion of diffuse light reaching Earth's surface, creating competing effects on plant growth. Analog studies using volcanic eruptions show impacts ranging from significantly negative to strongly positive, and numerical models suggest radiative effects from SAI would range from neutral to slightly positive. Here we show, using eddy covariance measurements at eight AmeriFlux sites (four maize and four forest), that radiative effects of smoke are positive across sites. This suggests that radiative effects from SAI would likely be modest but positive, consistent with numerical models. We attribute inconsistencies in the literature to limitations in the underlying assumptions and methods of previous analog studies; addressing these issues brings their results into agreement with our findings. More broadly, our results suggest that aerosols from wildfires, volcanoes, pollution, and SAI tend to moderately enhance photosynthesis.

item.title: Stabilized negative viscosity governs ocean jets before, during and after they leave the coast
item.dc:creator: Boris Galperin, Alexei Chekhlov, Ilya Staroselsky, Semion Sukoriansky
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: reanalysis, satellite altimetry
arXiv:2611.24399v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Eddies in rotating turbulence can feed the jets that spawn them, resulting in the negative viscosity phenomenon. Taken alone, a negative viscosity represents up-gradient eddy fluxes and is often referred to as "antifriction" or "antidiffusion". Mathematically, it leads to an ill-posed problem. In two-dimensional turbulence theory, this problem can be resolved by representing the transfer from small to large scales by a stabilized negative viscosity (SNV), in which a negative Laplacian viscosity is balanced by its positive biharmonic counterpart. In purely two-dimensional turbulence, by the Taylor identity, a negative viscosity is up-gradient transport of vorticity, which mixing cannot produce; on a slope, mixing of potential vorticity can mimic it, and we test for this. Using two years of wide-swath satellite altimetry (SWOT), we measure the eddy momentum flux across the five subtropical western boundary currents in each current's own frame. Along the continental slope the eddies act with a negative viscosity of order $-10^{3}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$, with the SNV structure resolved in the Gulf Stream and the Agulhas. At separation from the slope the sign reverses in all five currents, and the eddies brake the flow. Downstream, in the free jets, the negative viscosity returns on the cyclonic flank, strengthened to $-10^{4}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$. Separation is where the current leaves the strong topographic $\beta$ of the slope, the constraint that orders the eddy transfer. In an eddy-resolving reanalysis the SNV form holds across three ocean basins, with its shape parameter set by the deformation radius.

item.title: Impacts of snowpack on winter ecosystem respiration across the Northern Hemisphere
item.dc:creator: Bo Tang, Pengfeng Xiao, Xueliang Zhang, Hao Liu, Yantao Liu, Petri Pellikka, … (+2)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: snowpack
This study reveals how snowpack in the Northern Hemisphere shapes winter ecosystem respiration. Capturing that relation requires integrating multiple snowpack properties (depth, density, duration), rather than depth alone. Snowpack influences respiration through distinct environmental pathways (direct, thermal, and moisture), and exhibits strong regional differentiation. These complex mechanisms provide vital insights for refining global climate-carbon feedback predictions.

item.title: Detecting Climate Change Trends in a Snow‐Dominated Mediterranean Watershed
item.dc:creator: Cynthia Andraos, Yvonne Chloe El‐Kareh
item.description:
International Journal of Climatology — matched: reanalysis, climate change
Climate warming is altering snow dynamics and hydrological processes in Mediterranean mountain watersheds. This study develops a data‐driven framework to detect climate‐induced changes in the snow‐dominated Nahr Ibrahim watershed, Lebanon, by evaluating long‐term trends in climatic, snow‐related and hydrological parameters. Remotely sensed MODIS snow‐cover products, ERA5‐Land climate reanalysis and GloFAS discharge reanalysis are used to construct daily time series of snow cover area, precipitation, air temperature, relative humidity and river discharge for hydrological years 2000–2024. Annual and seasonal indicators are derived and analysed for monotonic trends using the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope estimator, while the Pettitt change‐point test is used to detect regime shifts. Innovative Trend Analysis (ITA) is applied as a complementary method that compares the two halves of the record. The most robust signal is a significant positive trend in annual mean air temperature (≈ +0.07°C year −1 ) accompanied by a significant regime shift in 2015, reflecting a transition to a warmer climate. Snow‐season onset exhibits a significant delay of roughly 1 day per year, whereas declines in maximum snow cover, snow persistence, snow‐season duration, melt timing and river discharge are evident but not statistically significant under the standard Mann–Kendall framework. Annual precipitation and mean relative humidity show no significant long‐term trends. ITA confirms the warming and the delayed snow‐season onset, and indicates that the decline in snow persistence, although not significant as a monotonic trend, is consistent across low, medium and high values. These results demonstrate that warming and delayed snow accumulation are the clearest climate‐change signatures in the Nahr Ibrahim watershed, while changes in snow extent and runoff remain concealed over the 25‐year record.

item.title: Enhancing data-driven weather forecasting via gated relative position encoding and spatial-aware feed-forward network
item.dc:creator: Leyi Wang, Duo Zhang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Baoxiang Pan, Dazhi Xi, Xiaoyu Huang
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
We develop two approaches to improve artificial intelligence weather forecasting. The first allows the model to adjust spatial relationships according to evolving atmosphere, while the second captures interactions between atmospheric variables and the lasting influence of geographic features such as terrain. Together, these approaches improve forecasts of key weather variables for several days ahead with only a small increase in computational cost.
